title: LIBS 7102 · Lecture 3
subtitle: Rejecting ethical relativism: the relativist's claims, why we should judge, Rachels's six claims and the cultural differences argument, shared values, objectivism vs absolutism, and tolerance
description: Lecture 3 of LIBS 7102: Microsoft and Strontium and the relativist's two claims; hypermoralism, relativism and getting tolerance just right; "do not judge" and the appeal to hypocrisy; Rachels's six claims, descriptive vs normative relativism, why the cultural differences argument is invalid and the three unacceptable consequences; less disagreement than it seems and the values all cultures share; Pojman's definitions of objectivism and absolutism, being an objectivist vs being objective, circumstantialism and the four-box diagram; why an objectivist can be tolerant. Practice answers R1 to R5 and an 18-item mock quiz.
intro:
:::exam Midterm facts
**Midterm: Wednesday Oct 28, in class.** Closed book, two hours, on paper, 20 % of the course. You write four or five two-paragraph answers, choosing from about six (for example, answer 4 of 6). Questions cover lectures 1 to 5 and are taken from the practice list (rare) or very similar to it (typical), often paired with a computing case or asking you to argue a side. It feeds the five relativism practice questions (R1 to R5), including the objectivism-vs-absolutism question the practice list warns about.
:::

chapters.title: 1. The relativist and why we judge

lessons.title: The relativist says no culture's morality is better than another's
"Do not judge" defeats itself, and hypocrisy does not make a judgment wrong
Cultures differ in their moral codes, but relativism does not follow
Cultures disagree less than they seem to and share core values
Objectivism asks whether there is a moral fact; absolutism whether a rule is never broken
An objectivist can be tolerant; a relativist cannot defend tolerance
